newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil soybean growers say weather mostly normal.
newsitem.headline: Brazil soybean growers say weather mostly normal.

text.p: Weather conditions were normal in most Brazilian soybean growing regions although some areas had not received water for several weeks and were reaching a critical point, agronomists said.
A cold front brought rains to many parts of Rio Grande do Sul and Parana this week, restoring moisture in areas which were becoming a little dry.
But the rains were patchy and some cooperatives in Rio Grande do Sul reported that a severe water shortage was blocking the development of the soybeans.

"The soybean has stopped developing because humidity is very low," said Aurio Zanatta, agronomist at the Cotriba cooperative in Ibiruba. "We haven't had any rain since Dec 20. We need rain right away."
Most of the soybean crop was still in the vegetative growth stage, agronomists said.
In Mato Grosso, 70 percent of the crop was in the vegetative growth stage while 30 percent was flowering, said Luiz Duarte at the Mato Grosso agricultural secretariat.
The state will start harvesting a small amount of soybeans at the end of January and is forecast to produce around five million tonnes in 1996/97.
"Thank goodness everything is going well here," Duarte said. "Conditions are normal."
Most analysts continued to expect a record 1996/97 crop of 26.5 to 27 million tonnes, saying the weather had been ideal in most areas until now.
A USDA estimate putting Brazil's 1996/97 soybean crop at 26 million tonnes was seen as conservative, even though farmers planted a smaller area than originally expected due to lack of financing.
On the export side, traders were unable to confirm reports that China may have bought Brazilian soybean oil this week.
According to U.S. vegetable oil dealers, China bought 20,000 to 30,000 tonnes of soyoil either from Argentina or Brazil, possibly from both, for January and February shipment.
Some traders thought Brazil did not have enough carry-over from the last harvest to cover this amount.
"I'll be very surprised if they get that much volume out of Brazil," said one trader. "I would imagine it would be a combined Argentine/Brazilian vessel."
Brazil still had a little bit of soymeal and soyoil left, but would have trouble delivering an order of that size until the new crop became available in March, the trader added.
"I don't think Brazil has a carry-over of 20,000 tonnes," agreed another.
A third dealer said he thought Brazil had enough soyoil to cover the order but China was more likely to have bought from Argentina.
"The free-on-board (FOB) price is cheaper in Argentina than in Brazil," he said. "Loading costs in Brazil are five times more expensive than in the U.S. and twice as expensive as in Argentina."
The government's foreign trade department said China had bought a total of 764,000 tonnes of Brazilian soyoil between January and December 1996, worth $409 million FOB.
It also bought 967,000 tonnes of soymeal for $242 million and 15,000 tonnes of soybeans for $4.3 million, both FOB.
